Chapter 2. The Rise of Shareholder Value and the Decline of Long-Term Thinking.
Picture this: inside boardrooms all across the country, there’s a new rallying cry—maximize shareholder value. On the surface, it sounds straightforward... even admirable, right? After all, shouldn’t companies look out for the people who own them? But as this idea took hold, something changed. Decisions started to shift in ways that left employees, customers, and even entire communities behind.
Take the story of a product designer at what used to be an innovative tech company. Meetings that once crackled with excitement about big ideas and new features? They turned into sessions laser-focused on cutting costs and hitting those quarterly numbers. The pressure for instant results was everywhere. Projects that needed time to grow—maybe years—were pushed aside for things that could deliver a quick win. That thrill of creating something new slowly faded, replaced by a nagging anxiety as the next earnings call loomed.
This shift wasn’t just a fluke. Back in the 1980s, a fresh wave of thinking swept through business schools and executive suites. The message was clear: a company exists, first and foremost, to serve its shareholders. The best way to do that? Zero in on short-term profits. Executives started getting stock options, so their pay rose and fell with the company’s share price. The theory was—if the stock did well, everyone would win.
But real life is rarely that simple. With so much riding on next quarter’s numbers, leaders started making decisions that looked good for the stock price in the short run—even when they chipped away at the company’s future. Factories closed. Workers got laid off. Research budgets shrank. And those savings? They showed up fast on the balance sheet, making the stock pop. But, little by little, the company’s ability to innovate and stay competitive slipped away.
It wasn’t just one company. Soon, buybacks became the norm—businesses using their own cash to snap up shares and push prices higher. Investors loved it, but it didn’t actually create anything new. Money that could’ve gone into fresh ideas, better training, or paying employees more? It went right back to shareholders and top executives instead.
The ripple effects were everywhere. Workers who once counted on stable jobs suddenly faced uncertainty. Whole communities, once anchored by local employers, watched as factories closed and storefronts emptied. That promise of shared prosperity—of everyone moving forward together—felt like it was slipping away, replaced by fragility and a sense of loss.
So, here’s the key takeaway. The obsession with shareholder value came at a real cost. Chasing short-term gains meant sacrificing what made companies strong in the long run. Businesses that once led the world in innovation and quality now found themselves struggling to keep up. The rewards flowed to a lucky few at the top, while everyone else was left picking up the pieces.
